item.title: Solid-state emissive acceptors enable thermally accessible radiative pathways for efficient organic solar cells
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02009-8 Solid-state emissive guest acceptors enhance organic solar cells by establishing thermally accessible radiative pathways, significantly reducing non-radiative voltage loss end enabling ternary blend devices with a certified power conversion efficiency of 20.84%.

item.title: Stable deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes with reduced efficiency roll-off via accelerated exciton utilization
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02029-4 Deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes leveraging phosphor-assisted TADF-sensitized fluorescence enable accelerated exciton dynamics, resulting in devices with an external quantum efficiency of 35.9% and an LT80 lifetime of 632 h.

item.title: Phase control of interfering stimulated Raman pathways in the XUV regime
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02024-9 Researchers modulate population transfer from the helium ground state to a metastable state by controlling the relative phase between two interfering stimulated Raman pathways through the continuum, demonstrating phase-coherent control in the extreme ultraviolet.

item.title: High-entropy molecular contacts enable high-efficiency and stable perovskite solar cells
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02028-5 High-entropy molecular contacts made by blending self-assembled molecules improve hole transport through diverse packing modes. Solar cells incorporating these contacts achieve a certified power conversion efficiency of 27.31% and negligible loss after 1,300 h of operation at 85 °C.

item.title: Engineering the unknown: building vacuum and cryogenic systems for the quantum frontier
item.description: Qubit decoherence remains the primary barrier to many practical quantum devices. This is why vacuum and cryogenic equipment scaling are key enablers to delivering useful quantum products and systems The post Engineering the unknown: building vacuum and cryogenic systems for the quantum frontier appeared first on Physics World .

item.title: Jamming the flow to enable memory in quantum materials
item.description: Understanding and controlling phase transitions are fundamental to physics and central to many technological revolutions. There is currently strong interest in materials with coupled structural and electronic phase transitions, where controlling the transition plasticity naturally yields built-in memory—a key step in emulating neurons and synapses for "neuromorphic" or brain-like computing technologies.

item.title: Ultrashort laser pulses offer a new way to probe electrons' quantum geometry
item.description: Researchers at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and the University of Regensburg have developed a method for determining, using light, a quantum property of electrons that has hitherto been difficult to access. The focus is on what is known as Berry curvature—a quantity that describes certain geometric properties of the quantum mechanical states of electrons. item.description: Researchers propose a new way to search for physics beyond the Standard Model by studying quantum-entangled quark pairs produced in electron-positron collisions The post Using quantum entanglement to probe hidden properties of quarks appeared first on Physics World .

item.description: A faster way of finding the best diamond-based materials for quantum computers has been developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL). The new approach has already identified promising materials for practical quantum sensors and computers that could one day transform scientific research as a whole. item.title: Quantum physicists trace a century of controlling spin
item.description: A concept from the field of quantum mechanics, spin is a property of particles that has no direct counterpart in everyday experience. Since the early 20th century, researchers have learned to manipulate it deliberately by means of precisely shaped electromagnetic pulses. item.title: ‘Cooked’ fiber doubles range of ultralow-noise supercontinuum lasers
item.description: After heating an optical fiber for nearly an hour, researchers completely changed its dispersion within a small section and ended up with a supercontinuum that covers a wide range of wavelengths—0.86 to 2.90 µm—and it’s also remarkably stable and reliable.

item.description: Recent research shows that gravity and quantum information are deeply connected and that the shape of spacetime can be traced back to the way information is stored in quantum fields.

item.title: From nonmagnetic to magnetic: A 2D semiconductor with electrically tunable magnetism
item.description: Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS), in collaboration with scientists from institutions in Switzerland, the Czech Republic and Germany, have demonstrated a way to introduce magnetism into an otherwise nonmagnetic two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor and subsequently control its magnetic properties using an electrical voltage. The findings, published in Science Advances, establish a new platform for investigating electrically controllable magnetism in atomically thin materia

item.title: One step closer to quantum computers that can correct their own mistakes
item.description: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions have shown that a quantum computer can check what is happening inside it and respond while it is running, repeatedly resetting parts of the system to bring chaotic behavior under control.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computers could finally get to grips with light and matter
item.description: Many of nature's most important processes depend on how particles of matter interact with light and other force-carrying particles. So far, however, it has proven difficult for conventional computers to determine how individual particles behave in these interactions.

item.title: Ultraviolet laser pulses engineer diamond defects selectively, leaving quantum qubits intact
item.description: When we think about a diamond, we often think about a material whose value comes from its perfection. In my research, however, I am interested in something almost opposite: the tiny imperfections inside diamonds. These atomic-scale defects can give diamonds new optical and electronic properties, and some of them can serve as quantum systems. The challenge is learning how to control these defects without disturbing the others.

item.title: New stability rules distinguish quantum phases of matter that an older method wrongly groups together
item.description: Most of us recognize basic phases of matter and their properties: solids maintain their shape, liquids flow freely with constant volume, and gases expand to fill their container. Quantum phases, on the other hand, are much harder to categorize, overturning traditional notions of what a phase even is and forcing physicists to rethink their definitions.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computer observes foundational quantum effect in a new setting
item.description: Physicists in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford have used a hybrid quantum computer, made up of qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation. The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by traveling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.

item.title: Quantum chip holds multiple photons at once, opening path to scalable memory
item.description: For highly fragile quantum information systems, the ability to store quantum information is vital—but also challenging. Quantum information is transported in particles of light called photons, which often must be temporarily paused (or "stored") while other, slower quantum operations catch up. This storage must be performed on microchips as small as 1 centimeter (0.4 inches)—a distance covered by light in a few trillionths of a second. Storing photons for a microsecond would represent a massive

item.title: Light reads electron spins inside porous crystals, opening path to quantum chemical sensors
item.description: University of Glasgow researchers are part of an international collaboration that could lead to a new generation of quantum sensors. The team, which included researchers from the University of Tokyo, University of Glasgow, University of Sheffield and Kobe University, has for the first time used light to read out the magnetic spin of electrons trapped inside a porous crystalline material known as a metal-organic framework (MOF).

item.title: Lensless imaging method enables long-term monitoring of living cells without staining
item.description: In a study led by Tampere University, researchers have developed a new lensless imaging method that produces precise quantitative data on living cells from a single image. The compact system can be placed inside a standard cell-culture incubator, allowing living cells to be monitored continuously for hours or even days without staining or other labels. The research is published in the journal Applied Physics Letters.

item.title: Layered semiconductor unlocks magnetic control of light emitted by quantum condensates
item.description: Quantum technologies are considered key technologies of the future. However, research in this field requires not only scientific expertise but sometimes also highly specialized laboratory conditions. Bose–Einstein condensates are a remarkable example, in which atoms move in lockstep, making quantum-mechanical effects visible not only at the level of individual atoms but also on a macroscopic scale. item.title: Quantum 'birthmarks' hold lasting traces of a system's past
item.description: Some classical physical systems can explore many configurations over time until their long-term behavior no longer reveals their starting conditions. The sampling of available configurations according to the appropriate statistical distribution is a property called ergodicity.

item.title: Ultrafast core-level spectroscopy reveals elusive precursors of exciton condensation in quantum materials
item.description: Many fascinating phases in quantum materials emerge when electrons, atoms and other microscopic components begin to act collectively. But these phases do not necessarily appear out of nowhere when a material crosses a transition temperature. Before long-range order develops, microscopic fluctuations can already be present.

item.title: Superconducting circuit links smaller photon groups into larger entangled states
item.description: Quantum computers, computer systems that leverage the laws of quantum mechanics, store and process information using qubits (i.e., quantum bits). In many quantum computers, qubits are linked via entanglement, a quantum mechanical effect that connects particles in such a way that their shared state cannot be described as separate, independent states.

item.title: How researchers tell different quantum excitations apart in individual molecules
item.description: Molecules can be placed in a wide variety of quantum states. How can these states be distinguished in measurements when theoretical models are unreliable? Which excitation process lies behind which measurement signal?
